title: Orbital CTO Andrew Thompson on Practice Area AI, Real Estate Law, and the Future of Legal Work
author: Andrew Thompson

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: Thompson shifts the emphasis from whether human oversight provides effective control and independent judgment to whether an identifiable human remains accountable. His regulated-domain and pilot analogy supports retaining a human presence, but does not address the cluster’s concern that accountability alone may lack usable information, intervention capacity or genuine control.
qs: Being accountable, again, really important in a sort of regulated domain when there’s insurance involved.
Maybe that will change in the future, but I think having humans being accountable is important.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Thompson contrasts lawyers’ years of experience with models’ embedded domain knowledge and argues for specialised tools, but the supplied excerpt does not address whether automation undermines associate apprenticeship, creates a verification-expertise paradox, or requires reconstructed training.
qs: Humans…  do take years to train and sort of years, sometimes decades on the job experience to gain all that experience.
A lot of that, not everything, a lot of that is sort of built inside the model.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Thompson describes regional adoption, fixed-fee real-estate work and a document-intensive US title-and-survey workflow, but does not address whether automation weakens apprenticeship, leverage or partner succession. The workforce questions are interviewer prompts, and the excerpt contains no answer from Thompson.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Thompson accepts the cluster’s core claim that specialist legal value lies in the workflow and tooling around improving general models. He materially extends it with a real-estate-specific “last mile” thesis: useful agentic products require redesigned interfaces, proprietary knowledge and hyper-specialised tools, while his capability expectations remain prospective rather than measured.
qs: It requires not just prompting the model better, it requires sort of proprietary knowledge or some of the tools that you’re giving it.
They need to be hyper specialized for sort of the real estate practice area.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Thompson accepts the cluster’s core account of jagged, task-specific capability and human-led work redesign, then materially extends it with a concrete real-estate deployment model: layer proprietary domain knowledge and specialised tools over general models, combine AI with classical technical methods for reliability, and have managers orchestrate both human and AI resources while humans retain accountability.
qs: It requires not just prompting the model better, it requires sort of proprietary knowledge or some of the tools that you’re giving it.
I’m orchestrating humans, but I’m also orchestrating tokens.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Thompson supports the cluster’s central proposition that practical legal AI depends on combining model capabilities with practice-specific knowledge, instructions and specialised tools. His account also reinforces the difficulty of the final mile, while offering illustrative development experience rather than validated performance evidence; it does not materially address evaluation, client-specific judgment or human checkpoints.
qs: How do you instruct it to think like in our case, a real estate lawyer, and then what specific tools do you need to give them in order to be sort of vastly better than the sort of general tools?
It requires not just prompting the model better, it requires sort of proprietary knowledge or some of the tools that you’re giving it.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s shift away from product announcements alone by emphasizing the need to inspect rapidly changing offerings, treating specialist-versus-general platform competition as unresolved, and cautioning that AI efficiency does not make billing-model change inevitable. It provides contextual market claims rather than evidence of realized value or superior performance.
qs: are moving faster, evolving faster than ever before and dropping new features all the time.
And it’s been incredibly persistent through year after year after year of people calling that the billable hour is going down.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Thompson directly supports the cluster’s emphasis on selective filtering amid information overload and on looking beyond legal technology—especially to software engineering—for early signals of emerging AI capabilities. His contribution is experiential rather than empirical and does not independently validate the reliability of his preferred sources.
qs: It’s like, I feel like I’m just have a ⁓ fire hose connected to my brain and I have to just sort of do filtering of like what’s important, what’s not.
And again, for this audience, if you want to see where the bleeding edge is at, look at software engineering.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Thompson’s account is consistent with the cluster’s view that legal-AI adoption is use-case-specific and shaped by existing workflows, pricing contexts and institutional response. His US title-and-survey example illustrates selective workflow-focused implementation, while the fixed-fee observation is relevant to pricing diversity. However, the source offers only qualitative product-leadership claims and does not substantively address verification, apprenticeship or market-wide economic effects.
qs: There’s a lot of fixed fee work, especially in real estate.
There’s often sometimes hundreds of exceptions and linked documents that you need to download and review.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Thompson supports the cluster’s proposition that AI’s value depends on organisational adaptation and continued human contribution. He specifically frames management as coordinating people and AI, while reinforcing the cluster’s conclusion that efficiency pressures hourly billing without establishing what will replace it.
qs: I’m orchestrating humans, but I’m also orchestrating tokens.
And so I can imagine, again, I don’t know what’s gonna happen with the billable hour.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Thompson supports the cluster’s core view that AI will reshape legal production through human-orchestrated automation rather than autonomous replacement of lawyers. His emphasis on practice-specific instruction, specialised tools and proprietary knowledge also aligns with the cluster’s focus on workflow design and institutional capability, although he is more bullish about the speed of agentic adoption and offers no firm pricing conclusion.
qs: This idea of of humans being able to…  ⁓ orchestrate a huge amount of AI agents to do far more work than was possible.
How do you instruct it to think like in our case, a real estate lawyer, and then what specific tools do you need to give them in order to be sort of vastly better than the sort of general tools?

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Thompson supports the cluster’s core complementarity account: AI can outperform humans on some legal activities while remaining weaker on others, and human accountability retains institutional value even where automation is technically capable. He does not materially substantiate the cluster’s staffing or employment implications.
qs: And I think now we’ve just layered in this new thing that sort of takes some of the things humans can do and it is much better than them, but it’s also sort of not as good in other things.
Maybe that will change in the future, but I think having humans being accountable is important.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that a crowded, fast-changing legal-AI market requires active product scrutiny rather than reliance on announcements alone. It also reinforces the unresolved competition between general-purpose model providers and specialist platforms, while offering vendor demonstrations as a practical—though not independently validated—selection aid.
qs: You know, we’re currently in a high stakes debate over whether the future of law belongs to the one model for everything giants or the specialized scalpel designed for specific practice areas.
One of the best ways of course to stay on top of technology in this crowded market is to see demos of new products and new product features.

kp.k: Orbital reports substantial specialist adoption and US expansion
kp.d: Thompson describes Orbital as real-estate-specific AI developed by technical experts and real estate lawyers. He reports approximately 200,000 US and UK property transactions last year, adoption by a majority of the top 20 real estate practices, and the US becoming its largest market. The hosts report a $60 million Series B financing. These are company and host claims, not independently evaluated adoption or performance findings.
qs: We did about 200,000 property transactions last year in the US and the UK.
We’ve got the majority of sort of the top 20 real estate practices using Orbital.
we started in the UK, we’ve now gone to the US, that’s our biggest market

kp.k: Deep specialization complements rather than replaces general intelligence
kp.d: Responding to the hosts’ framing of competition from foundation-model legal plugins, Thompson advocates a barbell approach combining improving general models with deeply specialized tools, data and instructions. He argues that lightly differentiated applications risk being eclipsed by model upgrades, whereas difficult remaining workflow requirements demand proprietary domain knowledge. His 80%/20% split is explicitly illustrative, not a measured success rate.
qs: I think about it sort of this barbell approach.

You can sort of start with something general and build something sort of light on top. And yeah, you’re a little bit better than the general, but you’re almost…  at threat is as each time they get better and better, you very quickly get eclipsed.
I’m just sort of cherry picking here, but 80 % of the solution.
but that last 20 % is really hard. It requires not just prompting the model better, it requires sort of proprietary knowledge or some of the tools that you’re giving it.

kp.k: AI products must anticipate continuing model improvements
kp.d: Thompson recommends building useful products for expected improvements in model cost, intelligence, capability and speed over six, 12 and 18 months, rather than optimizing only for present limitations. He characterizes this as different from conventional SaaS development and uses the desktop-to-mobile transition as an analogy for redesigning user experience rather than transferring old interfaces unchanged. He acknowledges uncertainty about the pace and direction of progress.
qs: One of the mantras we have is sort of betting on the model.
I think the game you need to play is like betting on the model, build something that’s valuable today, but also in six months and 12 months.
And that is surprisingly different from building SaaS software.
you’re not entirely sure all the time where, like how fast the world is going to move in what trajectory.

kp.k: Spatial automation connects legal descriptions to physical property
kp.d: Thompson describes extracting property descriptions from documents of variable quality, interpreting them as points, lines and curves, and plotting boundaries using conventional computational methods. AI orchestrates these steps alongside visual analysis and computer vision. He claims this automates work that typically takes humans hours, but supplies no timed comparison or error-rate study.
qs: there’s a reasoning challenge on sort of turning what is typically sort of textual legal description of the property into a collection of essentially points and lines and curves.
You’ve sort of done the extraction and now you’re sort of plotting it on a map.
You can now get AI to do that all automatically, where it’s sort of piecing all of those pieces together that typically would take hours for a human to do manually.

kp.k: Reliable visual workflows still require hybrid technical systems
kp.d: Thompson says visual language models currently struggle with complex real estate surveys and plans, so Orbital combines them with OCR, classical machine learning and computer vision to improve accuracy and reduce hallucinations. He attributes some limitations to scarce accessible domain-specific image data, while qualifying his account of model training as partly speculative and noting Orbital does not train its own VLM. Replacement of these hybrid systems by stronger VLMs is a future possibility, not a current capability.
qs: But if you take a picture of a very complex real estate survey or plan, you know, it just sort of falls over.
These documents still need to be OCR’d.
VLMs have their strength over classical machine learning and classical machine learning has its strength over VLMs and sort of the two together are great.

very detailed, real estate specific, legal images that are buried in 100 page PDFs that are private information. The Model Labs don’t have access to that and so they just can’t reason well over those images yet.
Long term, you can imagine the same thing that happened with sort of LLMs will happen with VLMs, but we’re not quite there today.

kp.k: Durable domain instructions outlast model-specific prompting tricks
kp.d: Thompson distinguishes reusable legal workflow knowledge from prompts overfitted to a particular model. Orbital’s US and UK lawyers encode principles such as resolving inconsistent property descriptions and boundaries at an abstraction level intended to survive upgrades. He reports that motivational prompting tricks are becoming unnecessary and that models increasingly help update the prompt library, reducing his earlier concern about a growing maintenance burden. No quantified maintenance savings or hallucination results are supplied.
qs: if you get that wrong, you specify it so specifically that each new model, you have to change a huge amount.
What happens when you have two legal descriptions that don’t match related to the same property?
A lot of that stuff is just melting away into nothing, and you no longer have to do that.
we can take our prompt library, feed it to these models, and just iteratively go on and say, this is what we’re finding from one model to the next. Help us update all of these prompt libraries.

kp.k: US localization involves security, billing and title workflows
kp.d: Thompson reports broadly shared UK and US client priorities: faster responses, high quality, an additional check and risk reduction. Differences include UK emphasis on ISO 27001 versus SOC 2, data residency requirements, greater US reliance on hourly billing, and more fixed-fee UK real estate work. He describes US firms as initially more conservative following an unspecified ABA AI ruling, with committees subsequently narrowing that adoption gap. Title and survey review, including potentially hundreds of exceptions and linked documents and interaction with title companies, required substantial US-specific product development.
qs: They want a second pair of eyes on everything.
ISO 27001, you know, much more prevalent here in the UK versus SOC 2.
The billable hour, lot more prevalence in the US than in the UK.
There’s a lot of fixed fee work, especially in real estate.
A lot of large US law firms have committees to handle that. So I think that’s becoming ⁓ less of a difference between the two regions.
You get a title commitment policy. There’s often sometimes hundreds of exceptions and linked documents that you need to download and review.

kp.d: Asked whether specialization could reduce energy consumption, Thompson explicitly disclaims a definitive answer. He reasons that fewer tokens could reduce computation and that domain expertise might improve efficiency, but large property portfolios still require extensive reading. His example is a thousand properties, each with 10 documents of 50 to 100 pages. He expects most efficiency gains below the application layer, from GPUs and model algorithms, rather than asserting demonstrated energy savings from Orbital.
qs: I don’t think I’m educated enough to know categorically the answer on that actually.
The more tokens you use, the more GPUs are crunching them, the more energy you’re using.
I think ultimately where the efficiency comes from more is sort of a layer below the application stack.
That would be my sort of just thinking on the spot response to that.

kp.k: AI-native formation may alter expectations and creative capabilities
kp.d: Drawing on teaching 30 eleven-year-olds two years earlier and observing his now-thirteen-year-old son, Thompson argues that children can approach AI without adults’ investment in established manual workflows. He reports his son building applications and games at an earlier age than he himself could, and predicts greater AI fluency on entry into university and employment. These are personal anecdotes and expectations, not systematic evidence about future lawyers or workforce outcomes.
qs: That was two years ago when my son was 11.
You know, I’ve got a lot of my career and reputation built on doing something in a bit more of a manual way. Children don’t have any of that, right?
He can code up things now that I wasn’t even doing in university. And he was doing that when he was 11.
by the time he goes to university and he gets into the job he’ll just be so AI native he’ll understand the world in a way that most of us sort of are still kind of grappling with

kp.k: Agent orchestration could transform work sooner than anticipated
kp.d: Against the host’s three-to-five-year scenario, Thompson predicts earlier widespread human orchestration of AI agents, using changes among his software engineers as an analogy for other industries. He expects cognitive capability, market knowledge and execution speed to become more broadly available. He invokes METR’s task-duration research, recalling progression from minutes to more than half a day or a day, but gives no specific study, test conditions or legal-task evidence and qualifies that recollection.
qs: I think three to five years is, like, it’s coming sooner.
I’m already seeing it with engineers on my team, back to this point around, look at what software engineers are doing, and probably that’s coming for lots of other industries.
METR M-E-T-R, is a research group that shows how this is sort of the exponential increase in terms of how much work can the equivalent AI system do that a human took N hours?
And it’s now sort of, I believe, you know, in the kind of more than half a day to more than a day worth of work

kp.k: Human value may shift toward accountability and orchestration
kp.d: Thompson identifies empathy, accountability and effective coordination of people and AI as possible continuing sources of professional value. He reports empathy as a recurring theme in customer and Legal Week conversations, emphasizes regulation and insurance, and uses a human airline pilot as an analogy for desired accountability despite automation. This is a tentative account of augmentation and changing roles, not a demonstrated occupational outcome or specific staffing-model prediction.
qs: talking to our customers, being at sort of legal week, human empathy seems to come up more and more.
As of yet, most AI systems can’t be regulated, they’re not insured, even if they are.
I think having humans being accountable is important.
I’m orchestrating humans, but I’m also orchestrating tokens.

kp.k: Efficiency pressures hourly billing without determining its replacement
kp.d: Thompson argues that AI creates an inherent conflict with billing for time by making work more efficient. He describes debate at Legal Week, reports clients asking to move away from hourly billing, and stresses the model’s persistence despite repeated predictions of its demise. He expressly declines to forecast what will happen to the billable hour or identify a settled replacement.
qs: I don’t know what’s gonna happen with the billable hour.
Now clients are asking for take it away.
And it’s been incredibly persistent through year after year after year of people calling that the billable hour is going down.
There is an inherent conflict with AI because it is making the work more efficient.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Thompson predicts that general models and deeply specialised practice-area platforms will coexist, while lightly differentiated legal software risks being eclipsed.
pts.d: Andrew Thompson describes a barbell rather than an either/or market. Orbital's proposed differentiation is domain-specific instructions, proprietary knowledge, tools and data layered over improving foundation models. He argues that generic AI can provide much of a solution, but completing difficult real-estate workflows requires specialisation. His 80/20 illustration is explicitly approximate, not a measured result.

pts.k: AI can automate real-estate boundary mapping that otherwise takes hours, but current systems require several complementary technologies.
pts.d: Thompson describes extracting textual legal descriptions, interpreting points, lines and curves, and plotting boundaries. AI orchestrates visual-language models, classical machine learning, computer vision, OCR and conventional mapping. He says visual models alone cannot yet reliably handle complex real-estate surveys and plans; combining techniques supports accuracy and reduces hallucinations. This is a claim about workflow automation, not a claim that legal transactions can proceed without human accountability.

pts.k: Improving models are reducing the maintenance burden of model-specific prompt tricks while making durable legal-domain instructions more valuable.
pts.d: Thompson distinguishes teaching the system real-estate workflows at an appropriate abstraction level from overfitting prompts to a particular model. He says the former accumulates value across upgrades, while tricks such as telling a model that an answer is important to one's career are becoming unnecessary. Orbital also uses models to help revise its prompt libraries, automating some internal engineering work.

pts.k: Thompson expects agent orchestration to expand lawyers' productive capacity sooner than three to five years, but does not predict the billable hour's demise.
pts.d: He extrapolates from engineers on his team to other industries, including legal services. As cognitive capabilities, knowledge and execution speed become more widely available, he identifies empathy, accountability and effective orchestration of humans and AI as possible sources of professional value. He recognises a conflict between efficiency and hourly billing but explicitly leaves the eventual pricing model unresolved.

pts.k: In a broader workforce observation, Thompson predicts AI-native entrants will start with capabilities and habits that established professionals must acquire.
pts.d: His basis is anecdotal: teaching children and observing his son's AI-assisted coding and app creation. He argues that children have less attachment to manual ways of working and can accomplish technical tasks earlier. The horizon is their future university attendance and employment, not a specific forecast about legal recruitment or jobs.

pts.k: Thompson tentatively expects most energy-efficiency gains to come from hardware and model algorithms rather than practice-area specialisation.
pts.d: He offers explicitly on-the-spot reasoning, not an empirical finding. Domain knowledge might reduce waste, but large real-estate portfolios still require processing extensive documents. He links application incentives to token costs and suggests the largest improvements occur below the application layer.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The specialist-platform and workflow claims primarily draw on Thompson's product-development experience and self-reported customer adoption.
pts.d: Thompson reports approximately 200,000 US and UK property transactions in the preceding year and adoption by a majority of the top 20 real-estate practices. He names customers including Seyfarth Shaw, BCLP, Vinson & Elkins, Goodwin and Polsinelli. These figures establish the scale he reports for Orbital's use; the interview supplies no comparative benchmark, measured accuracy rate or controlled time-saving study for its superiority or automation claims.

pts.k: The prompt-maintenance claim rests on internal experimentation; the agent-capacity forecast combines engineering observations with a reference to METR.
pts.d: Thompson says Orbital tried prompt techniques discussed in papers and observed results, without identifying studies or supplying a testing protocol. For longer task execution, he invokes METR research and tentatively recalls AI task horizons of more than half a day to more than a day. He does not identify a study version, task set, success threshold or legal-specific evaluation. His views on future human value draw on customer discussions and conversations at Legal Week.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Specialist advantage depends on continuing to add deep workflow value as foundation models improve; technical forecasts remain explicitly uncertain.
pts.d: In this 2026 interview, Thompson advocates building products that remain valuable over six-, twelve- and eighteen-month model-improvement cycles. He expects substantial improvement over coming years, but recognises uncertainty about its rate and direction. Hybrid visual processing is a present requirement in his account; eventual replacement by stronger visual models is a possibility rather than a dated commitment.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries described are US and UK real-estate lawyers and their clients, with region-specific adoption and workflow requirements.
pts.d: Thompson says lawyers in both markets seek faster responses, high quality, a second pair of eyes and reduced risk. He reports greater US reliance on hourly billing and more UK fixed-fee real-estate work. US firms were initially more conservative about AI, but he says committees have narrowed that difference. US title-and-survey review requires particular product functionality, including handling numerous exceptions and linked documents and working with title companies. His reference to an ABA ruling is not accompanied by a specific rule or opinion identifier.

pts.k: Lawyers and managers may increasingly contribute through accountability and AI orchestration rather than execution speed alone.
pts.d: Thompson envisages humans directing both people and AI systems. He presents empathy and accountability as possible continuing differentiators, particularly in regulated and insured services. This is an augmentation-oriented account: he does not forecast lawyer headcount, associate displacement, staffing shapes or autonomous replacement of the profession.
